summary: 제안 논문과 기존 논문은 모두 사전학습 언어모델의 설계가 다운스트림 성능에 미치는 영향을 다루며, BERT 계열 Transformer 인코더와 SQuAD·GLUE 같은 평가 축을 공유한다. 다만 제안 논문은 기존 논문의 핵심 기반 위에서 NSP 제거, FULL-SENTENCES 입력, 동적 마스킹, 더 큰 배치·더 긴 시퀀스 학습, byte-level BPE, 추가 데이터(CC-NEWS) 등 구체적 설계 선택지를 변형·확장한다.

제안 논문과 기존 논문은 모두 사전학습 언어모델의 설계가 다운스트림 성능에 미치는 영향을 다루며, BERT 계열 Transformer 인코더와 SQuAD·GLUE 같은 평가 축을 공유한다. 다만 제안 논문은 기존 논문의 핵심 기반 위에서 NSP 제거, FULL-SENTENCES 입력, 동적 마스킹, 더 큰 배치·더 긴 시퀀스 학습, byte-level BPE, 추가 데이터(CC-NEWS) 등 구체적 설계 선택지를 변형·확장한다.

caution_points: [M2 ↔ P2] Both papers explicitly address next sentence prediction in pretraining, so a reviewer may view the proposal as a modification of the same pretraining axis. Clarify that our work studies the effect of removing this objective under a re-optimized training setup rather than reusing the original objective.

[M4 ↔ P1] Both papers rely on masking-based pretraining, so dynamic masking may be read as a variant of the same MLM framework. Add a concrete explanation of how changing the masking pattern across training differs from the fixed masked language model setup.

[M5 ↔ P1] The use of dynamic masking can still look close to the prior masked language model objective because both optimize prediction of masked tokens. Strengthen the manuscript by stating where the masking schedule changes during training and why that changes the learning signal.

[M6 ↔ P2,P7,P8] FULL-SENTENCES without NSP loss may be seen as overlapping with the prior sentence-pair formulation using next sentence prediction and special tokens. Explain more explicitly that the proposal changes the input construction and training objective together, not just the surface formatting of sentence pairs.

[M8 ↔ P6] Both papers use subword-based input vocabularies, so a reviewer may regard this as a vocabulary-scale variant of the same embedding design. Distinguish the work by describing the byte-level BPE choice and its difference from the prior WordPiece setup.

[R-M1 ↔ R-P11] Both papers report SQuAD v1.1 dev single EM, so the scores are directly comparable. Pre-empt reviewer comments by stating that the comparison is made under the same evaluation condition while the training design differs.

[R-M2 ↔ R-P12] Both papers report SQuAD v1.1 dev single F1, which can invite a direct same-task comparison. Add brief text that frames the result as evidence under matched evaluation rather than as reuse of the same method.

[R-M3 ↔ R-P23] Both papers report SQuAD v2.0 dev single EM under the same condition, so reviewers can compare the numbers one-to-one. Clarify which training design changes are responsible for this matched-setting comparison.

[R-M4 ↔ R-P24] Both papers report SQuAD v2.0 dev single F1 under the same condition, which may amplify perceived overlap. Specify that the evaluation setup is shared but the pretraining design choices being tested are different.

[R-M5 ↔ R-P25] Both papers report SQuAD v2.0 test single EM under the same condition, enabling direct numeric comparison. Note explicitly that the comparison uses the same benchmark condition without additional training data.

[R-M6 ↔ R-P26] Both papers report SQuAD v2.0 test single F1 under the same condition, so reviewers may focus on score differences alone. Add wording that ties the difference to the revised pretraining configuration and data scale.
differentiation_suggestions: Our work does not keep the next sentence prediction objective; instead, it re-examines whether downstream gains depend on removing that objective under the same pretraining family. This makes the comparison about a specific training design choice rather than about introducing a different encoder architecture.

While the prior work uses a masked language model objective, our work changes the masking pattern dynamically during training. This focuses the contribution on the training procedure applied to the same pretraining paradigm, not merely on adopting masked token prediction itself.

Our work expands the pretraining setup with a larger byte-level BPE vocabulary and additional CC-NEWS data, whereas the prior work describes WordPiece embeddings and does not present a corresponding new dataset element in its core techniques. The distinction should be stated as a difference in input representation and data scope within the same general pretraining framework.
related_work_draft: The prior work (Devlin et al., arXiv, 2019) established BERT pre-training with masked language modeling and next sentence prediction using a bidirectional Transformer encoder. Our work builds on this pretraining family while revisiting specific design choices such as NSP removal, dynamic masking, input formatting, vocabulary, and training data scale.
